newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban fighters pause after seizing Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Taleban fighters pause after seizing Kabul.

text.p: Afghanistan's victorious Taleban Islamic militia paused in its pursuit of forces loyal to ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani who were apparently regrouping in the Panjsher Valley north of the capital Kabul.

Taleban instead concentrated on consolidating its hold over Kabul, where it set up a strict fundamentalist Moslem government after capturing the city against little resistance last Friday at the climax of a sweep through eastern Afghanistan.

A Pakistan-based private Afghan news service said Taleban had seized Charikar, capital of Parwan province north of Kabul, and were heading further north towards the Jabal-us-Seraj base of pro-Rabbani forces.

But reporters visiting the area said Rabbani's forces still controlled Charikar and Taleban fighters were making no attempt to advance from the Bagram military air base, 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul.

Four tanks flying Taleban's plain white flag guarded the edge of the militia's territory at Bagram. A score of Rabbani fighters manned a checkpoint just south of Charikar about 10 km (six miles) further north.
Taleban said earlier it believed Rabbani and his aides, abandoning Kabul, fled to Jabal-us-Seraj just before the militia's fighters took control of the capital.

A pro-Rabbani commander told reporters that Rabbani, his top military commander Ahmad Shah Masood, prime minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar and Abdurrab Rasul Sayyaf, leader of a pro-Rabbani faction, were now all in the Panjsher Valley in Kapisa province.
Masood's mainly ethnic Tajik forces, based in the Panjsher, were in the forefront of the guerrilla war against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in 1980s.
Rabbani had said in a statement on Friday his administration had moved from Kabul to Parwan and Kapisa and was controlling security and defence affairs from there.
He called on the world not to recognise the Islamic government decreed by Taleban, which has barred women from working in offices and promised death for adulterers and drinkers.

Pakistan has indicated that it may recognise the Taleban government but other countries, including the United States and China, took a more cautious line and appealed for reconciliation and an end to fighting.
Taleban fighters patrolled Kabul in pick-up trucks but there were no signs of tensions as the city resumed normal life after the Friday weekend.
A Taleban preacher at a mosque in Kabul's diplomatic Wazir Akbar Khan district said all men should wear either traditional skull caps or turbans to conform with strict Islamic tenets.
Official Kabul Radio urged those who had fled the capital fearing bloodshed to return and said government employees should report for work.
The radio also broadcast a message from Taleban's supreme leader, Mullah Mohammad Omar, saying his movement wanted good relations with all peace-loving countries.

United Nations special peace envoy Norbert Holl told Taleban officials in the southern town of Kandahar that he wanted to have good relations with the Islamic movement, the Afghan Islamic Press service quoted a Taleban spokesman as saying.
Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati urged groups in Afghanistan to share power and avoid outside interference in the country's affairs.
"No (Afghan) group could push out the other groups...All should learn to live side-by-side," Velayati told Iranian Television in a satelite link-up from New York.
